vignette:
He was thirty-six, married, and had worked at the same big-box retail store for nearly nine years. Most of his shifts were in the back warehouse—unloading trucks, stocking shelves, operating the pallet jack. It was a steady job, the kind of work that made his body tired and his mind quiet. That changed on the second weekend of December.

A transformer blew behind the store, then the electrical panel caught fire. He remembers the smell of melting plastic and the sound of the sprinklers going off—not the alarm, but the sprinklers. Water poured from the ceiling as smoke filled the aisles. He helped a new cashier get out through the fire door, then went back in to find the assistant manager, who was still near the electronics cage. The assistant manager was banging on the cage door, screaming. The steel handle was hot to the touch. He grabbed it anyway, burned his palm, and pulled the door open. They both ran.

That night he felt grateful. He had a slight burn and some smoke inhalation, but he was alive. The next morning he called his wife from the emergency room, his voice shaking, and he told her, "I almost didn't make it." She drove straight there, wrapped her arms around him, and he sobbed into her jacket.

That was eighteen months ago.

Now he cannot walk into the back warehouse. Every time he steps past the swinging double doors, his chest tightens and his breathing goes shallow. His supervisor has moved him to front-end customer service, which he hates because of the constant chatter and the fluorescent lights. But it keeps him away from the pallet jacks and the smell of cardboard and the memory of smoke.

At home, he has started sleeping on the living room couch. His wife has asked him why, gently, more than once. He tells her the bed is too soft, but really it is because he gets jolted awake at three in the morning with a dream of the sprinkler water hitting his face and the handle burning his palm. When he wakes, his hand still aches, even though the burn scars healed months ago. He does not want to wake her.

He has stopped watching television shows that contain any kind of explosion, fire, or sirens. He will pick up the remote and turn it off, or change the channel without explaining. His wife has learned not to ask. She has noticed he no longer wants to grill on the back patio, because the propane tank reminds him of the transformer. He says he is just tired of cleaning the grill.

At work, he has become short with customers. Twice this month a customer asked him for help finding an item, and he felt a wave of irritation so hot and sudden that he had to walk away mid-sentence. He told the first customer, "I can't help you," and turned around. His manager pulled him aside and asked if everything was all right. He lied and said he had a headache.

He does not talk about the fire. When his coworkers mention that night, he changes the subject or walks away. He told his wife he is fine, he just wants to move on. But he has not been able to sleep through the night in over a year. He checks the smoke detectors in his apartment every week, and he has bought three fire extinguishers—one for the kitchen, one for the hallway, one for the living room. She said, "Honey, we have enough." He said, "You never know."

At the grocery store, if he hears a fire truck siren, he will freeze. He will stand in the middle of an aisle, staring at a box of cereal, breathing slow and deliberate, until the sound fades. Sometimes it takes a full minute. People bump into him with their carts, and he does not flinch. He does not move. He just waits.

His wife is patient. She brings him tea at night and sits beside him on the couch. He wants to tell her that he loves her, that he is sorry, that he does not know why he cannot go into the warehouse or sleep in his own bed. But when he opens his mouth, his throat feels tight, and the smell of melted plastic comes back. So he says nothing. He holds her hand, and he stares at the wall, and he tries not to remember the way the sprinkler water tasted—chemical and hot—or the look on the assistant manager's face before the handle burned his hand. He tries, most days, to keep the memory far away. But it keeps finding him. In the buzz of the fluorescent lights, in the clatter of a metal cart, in the half-light before he wakes.
